title: The Tiger, the Brahman and the Jackal

setting.period: Folk-tale time in the Punjab, the land of five rivers

provenance.rights: The text is our own retelling of a traditional Punjabi folk tale, written for Omramo; it does not use the wording of the cited edition. The cited edition is in the US public domain (published before 1931); other territories not verified. Legal review pending (PRD Q23).

geography.lesson: The Punjab is a wide, flat farming land in the north of India and Pakistan, named for its five rivers. Wheat and mustard grow there, watered from rivers and wells.

culture.lesson: A Brahman is a Hindu priest and teacher; the story treats him simply as a gentle, learned man. In a village quarrel people ask others to judge, often elders sitting under a pipal tree. Tigers no longer live in the Punjab, but about three thousand still live wild in India, in protected forests.

moral.lesson: The Brahman's kindness is right, but he trusts tears and promises without thinking. The Jackal wins without a fight: he stays calm and lets the Tiger's pride and temper do the work.
moral.reflectionQuestion: Was the Brahman wrong to open the cage? What would you have done?

moral: Be kind with your eyes open, for a cool head beats a hot temper.

cover.alt: A sandy-gold jackal bows politely before a bamboo cage with a large tiger glaring out through the bars, while a thin old man in white stands by with his staff.

card.label: Character · a priest and teacher
card.title: The Brahman
card.body: He owns little more than a staff and a bundle, and he cannot bear to see anyone cry. A promise from him is a promise kept, even to a tiger.
card.portraitAlt: A thin, kindly old man in a plain white cotton dhoti and shawl, holding a wooden staff, with a small cloth bundle on his shoulder.

card.label: Character · the clever one of the fields
card.title: The Jackal
card.body: He is small and sandy-gold, and he would never win a fight with a tiger. So he wins with his wits, and looks as slow as he can.
card.portraitAlt: A slim sandy-gold jackal with pointed ears and a bushy tail, sitting with his head tilted and one paw raised to scratch his ear.

cultureNote.text: The name Punjab means “five waters” in Persian. Its rivers run down from the Himalaya mountains, and farmers there grow much of the wheat that India and Pakistan eat.

tapTargets.title: A Brahman
tapTargets.line: A Brahman is a Hindu priest and teacher who learns the old prayers and teaches them.

cultureNote.label: From India
cultureNote.text: In Hindu tradition, a Brahman’s work is to study, to teach and to lead the prayers at weddings and festivals. Indian folk tales often tell of a poor Brahman who is gentle and learned.

cultureNote.label: From the Punjab
cultureNote.text: Many people in India hold the pipal sacred, so it is not cut down lightly. Travellers rest in its shade, and village elders often meet under one to settle a quarrel.

paras: ^A tiger sat in a cage beside a dusty road.

It was a trap of strong bamboo, set by a village in the <tap:punjab>Punjab</tap>, the land of five rivers. The <name:tiger>Tiger</name> had roared at the bars and bitten the bars. The bars had not minded at all.

Along the road came a poor <name:brahman>Brahman</name>, with a staff in his hand and a cloth bundle on his shoulder. <say:tiger*>“Holy one! Kind one!”</say> cried the Tiger. <say:tiger>“Open this door!”</say>
<say:brahman*>“I think not, my friend,”</say> said the Brahman mildly. <say:brahman>“You would eat me.”</say>
<say:tiger*>“Eat you? Never! I would carry your bundle for the rest of my days!”</say>
Now a <tap:priest-and-teacher>Brahman</tap> is a priest and a teacher, and this one had a soft heart.
The Tiger wept. He swore by every stripe on his back that he would never harm so good a man. Great tears rolled down his nose.
So the Brahman lifted the latch. Out sprang the Tiger, not weeping now.
<say:tiger*>“What a simple man you are!”</say> he purred. <say:tiger>“I have sat in that box for days, and I am hollow. You shall be my dinner.”</say>
<say:brahman*>“Is that fair?”</say> said the Brahman, and his staff shook in his hand. <say:brahman>“Let us ask the first three we meet.”</say> The Tiger yawned and agreed.
<say:tiger*>“Go and ask,”</say> said the Tiger, stretching out in the dust. <say:tiger>“I shall wait here. A Brahman always keeps his word.”</say>
That was true, and a great nuisance. The Brahman walked until he came to an old <tap:pipal-tree>pipal tree</tap>, whose heart-shaped leaves shivered in the smallest breeze.
<say:brahman*>“Pipal tree, I let a tiger out of a trap, and now he wishes to eat me. Is that fair?”</say>
The leaves rustled crossly. “Fair? All day long travellers cool themselves under my leaves. Then they snap off my twigs for their goats and walk on. Do not come to me for thanks.”
One answer, and it was against him.
Farther on, he heard a creak and a splash. An old buffalo was plodding round a <tap:well-wheel>well-wheel</tap>, and with every turn a row of clay pots tipped water into a ditch for the wheat.
The Brahman told his trouble a second time. <say:brahman*>“Is that fair, mother buffalo?”</say>

The buffalo did not stop walking. “When I gave milk, they fed me the best seed cake and scratched my ears,” she said. “Now I am old, they tie me to this wheel and throw me scraps. Only a fool waits for thanks.”
Round she went again, and the pots went splash. Two answers, and both against him.
There was nobody left to ask but the road itself, so the Brahman bent down and asked it.

The road answered in a dry, dusty whisper. “Feet tramp on me all day, and hooves, and bullock carts with squealing wheels. I carry every one of them to market and home again. What do they leave me? Dust, and whatever spills from their sacks.”
<say:brahman*>“Three answers,”</say> said the Brahman, counting on his fingers, <say:brahman>“and not one for me.”</say>
He looked down the long pale road, which led away to anywhere he liked. Then he sighed, turned round, and started back to the Tiger. He had given his word.
^Halfway back, a <name:jackal>Jackal</name> came trotting out of the mustard field.
<say:jackal*>“Good day, teacher!”</say> said the Jackal. <say:jackal>“Why so sad? You look like a kite with its string cut.”</say>
So the <name:brahman>Brahman</name> told him everything: the cage, the tears, the promise, the tree, the buffalo and the road.
The Jackal scratched one ear. <say:jackal*>“How very muddling,”</say> he said. <say:jackal>“Would you say it again?”</say> The Brahman said it again. The Jackal scratched the other ear.
<say:jackal*>“It is no use. My head is a basket with a hole in it. Take me to the place, and perhaps I shall see what you mean.”</say>
The Tiger was waiting by the cage, sharpening his claws on a thorn tree.
<say:tiger*>“The shadows have grown a good deal since you left,”</say> he growled. <say:tiger>“And who is this? I asked for one dinner, not two.”</say>
<say:brahman*>“One moment more, my lord,”</say> said the Brahman. <say:brahman>“Only let me explain things to this jackal. It takes him a while to get hold of a thing.”</say>
The Jackal bowed very low and looked as slow as he could.
So the Brahman told the tale once more. He told it slowly. He put in every bit of it, even the buffalo’s scraps, and the Tiger’s tail began to twitch.

<say:jackal*>“My head is spinning like a potter’s wheel!”</say> wailed the <name:jackal>Jackal</name>, clutching his ears. <say:jackal>“Let me see. The Brahman sat in the cage, and down the road came my lord the Tiger…”</say>
<say:tiger*>“No, you donkey!”</say> roared the Tiger. <say:tiger>“It was I who sat in the cage!”</say>
<say:jackal*>“Of course! It was I who sat in the cage. No, that cannot be right. The cage sat in the bundle, and the bundle sat on the buffalo, and the buffalo lifted the latch…”</say>
<say:tiger*>“Leave the buffalo out of it!”</say> howled the Tiger.
<say:jackal*>“Then it is hopeless, my lord,”</say> sighed the Jackal. <say:jackal>“Eat your dinner. I shall never, never understand.”</say>

That was too much for the Tiger. <say:tiger*>“Then I shall <stretch>show</stretch> you!”</say> he roared. <say:tiger>“Use your eyes. Here stands the Tiger. There stands the Brahman. This is the cage. And the Tiger was inside it!”</say>
<say:jackal*>“Tiger, Brahman, cage,”</say> said the Jackal, pointing at the wrong one each time. <say:jackal>“But inside, my lord? How could so grand a tiger fit through so small a door?”</say>
<say:tiger*>“Like <pop:1.3>this</pop>, you fool!”</say> The Tiger bounded into the cage and glared out through the bars. <say:tiger>“Now do you see?”</say>
<say:jackal*>“As clear as well water,”</say> said the Jackal, and he dropped the latch. <pop:1.3>Clack!</pop>
The Tiger stared at the bars. The bars still did not mind at all.
<say:jackal*>“There,”</say> said the Jackal, dusting his paws. <say:jackal>“Now everything is back where the village put it. I do like things tidy.”</say>
The Brahman’s staff stopped shaking. He shouldered his bundle, and the two of them set off down the road together.
Behind them the Tiger sat down to think it over. At evening the villagers would come and carry the cage, tiger and all, deep into the forest, far from anybody’s goats.
The Brahman walked through the pipal’s shade with his eyes wide open, and beside him trotted the Jackal, grinning.

sourceNotes: This is our own retelling, written for Omramo, of a traditional Punjabi folk tale.
It is not the wording of any earlier edition.
Documented source: Joseph Jacobs, "Indian Fairy Tales" (1892), story IX,
Project Gutenberg ebook #7128, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/7128
(US public domain; other territories not verified).
Jacobs took it from Steel and Temple, "Wide-awake Stories" (pp. 116-20), first printed in the
Indian Antiquary, vol. xii: a tale collected in the Punjab by Flora Annie Steel.
The source was read (Gutenberg mirror, 7128.txt) for the order of events only; no sentence is copied.
Softened: the tiger does not seize the Brahman; his threat is comic ("You shall be my dinner").
The tree, the buffalo and the road are gruff, not cruel; the tree's "be a man" taunt is left out.
Left out: the pipe ash the road complains of; the second retelling on the road is one line;
the tiger's "our dinner" joke (replaced by our own "one dinner, not two").
Departures from the cited book: the source ends when the jackal shuts the door. Our last page is added:
the Brahman and the Jackal walk away, and the villagers will carry the caged tiger to the forest.
Added: the Brahman goes back because he gave his word (the source gives no reason for his return).
The Jackal's muddle is in our own words (kite, basket, potter's wheel, the buffalo, the small door);
in the source the jackal asks how the tiger got in, and what "the usual way" is.
The buffalo's feed is "seed cake" here; the source names cotton seed and oil cake.
Reviewer to check: the neutral wording about Brahmans in the text and on the card (no caste judgement);
"Punjab" as Persian for "five waters"; the pipal held sacred and elders meeting under it;
the well-wheel (Persian wheel, rahat) and "most farms use motor pumps today"; the Jackal's greeting
"teacher"; "my lord" for the tiger; kite flying as a Punjabi image; a bamboo trap in the Punjab;
"about three thousand wild tigers in India" and "no tigers in the Punjab today" (education lesson only).
SOURCE CHECK (18 Nov 2026, against Gutenberg #7128 on the mirror): the first draft kept several of the
source's turns of phrase in the three answers and in the muddle scene; they were reworded in the edit.
The muddle itself (who was in the cage?) is the plot of the traditional tale and stays; the jokes in it
(the bundle, the buffalo lifting the latch, 'I do like things tidy') are ours. A second echo check is due.
Further departures from Jacobs: his tree speaks of cattle (ours: goats); his tiger promises to serve as a
slave (ours: to carry the bundle); his jackal's greeting is a fish simile (ours: a kite); his tiger
sharpens teeth and claws with no tree named. Jacobs's end-note on Steel and Temple was not re-read.
Status: DRAFT. Text review pending. Cultural review (standard: Punjabi reader, India and Pakistan) pending.

palette.mood: Warm dusty gold and straw, pale hazy sky, fresh green wheat and a line of mustard yellow, with the tiger's orange as the one strong note; dry, sunny and good-humoured.

artBrief.light: One long day on the plain, from pale morning to late afternoon; one warm light from the upper left in every picture. The sky is always PALE (hazy cream, pale gold, soft peach in scene-road), never dark, so the dark text reads on every page.
world: The Punjab plain before 1850: completely flat to the horizon, no hills in view. Fields of young green wheat and bright yellow mustard, divided by low earth banks and narrow water ditches.
The road is unpaved pale earth, rutted by cart wheels, raised a little above the fields, with dust at its edges and scattered grain husks.

Trees: thorny kikar (acacia) with flat feathery crowns and dark trunks by the roadside; one huge old pipal (Ficus religiosa) with a pale grey ribbed trunk and heart-shaped leaves that end in a long thin tail-like tip. A low earth or brick platform round its foot is right.
The village is far off: low flat-roofed houses of sun-dried mud brick, the same colour as the earth, a few trees, a thread of cooking smoke. No domes, no palaces.

The trap is a box cage of thick bamboo poles and wooden beams lashed with rope, with a wooden door that drops or swings and a simple wooden latch on the outside. It stands on the ground by the road, big enough for the tiger to sit up in.

The well-wheel is a Persian wheel: a round brick well, a large upright wooden wheel over it carrying a loop of small red clay pots on ropes, turned through wooden gears by a horizontal beam. The buffalo is yoked to the beam and walks a worn circle. Water spills into a wooden trough and runs along an earth ditch to the wheat.
The buffalo is a water buffalo: dark slate grey, heavy, with swept-back curved horns, old and thin-hipped but dignified, not pitiful.

The jackal is the golden jackal of the Indian plains: sandy-gold with a darker back, slim legs, pointed ears, a narrow muzzle and a short bushy tail tipped dark. Smaller than a wolf, not a red fox. He goes on four legs; no clothes.

The tiger is a Bengal tiger: rich orange with black stripes, white cheeks, chest and belly, white spots behind the ears. Grand, vain and comic; never bloody, no bared-fang snarl aimed at the viewer. His tears on page 2 are big and theatrical.

Clothes of the time for a poor Brahman: a plain white cotton dhoti and a white cotton shawl over one shoulder, a thin white sacred thread across the chest from the left shoulder (draw it simply, as one line), bare feet or plain wooden sandals. A wooden staff and a small bundle tied in faded cloth.
Small true details welcome: a paper kite far off in the sky in scene-road, bullock-cart ruts, a few goats near the far village, green parakeets or a hoopoe in the pipal.

Avoid: the Taj Mahal or any monument, elephants and maharajas, jewelled turbans, snake charmers, palm-tree jungle, Himalayan peaks behind the fields, a metal-barred zoo cage, religious images or shrines, caricatured faces, anything bloody or frightening.

characters.brahman: A thin, kindly older man, about three heads tall, brown skin, a shaved head with a small tuft of grey hair at the back, gentle small eyes and a mild smile. Plain white cotton dhoti and shawl, a simple sacred thread, bare feet. Signature details: the wooden staff (it trembles when he is afraid) and the small faded cloth bundle on his shoulder.
characters.jackal: A slim sandy-gold golden jackal with big pointed ears, a narrow muzzle and a bushy dark-tipped tail. Bright, knowing eyes that he keeps half shut when playing the fool. Signature gestures: scratching one ear with a hind paw, a very low bow, and a wide grin on the last page.
characters.tiger: A large Bengal tiger, broad-chested and proud, with fine white whiskers he is vain about. Sulky in the cage, sugary when begging, purring and lordly when free, puffed up with temper in Part II. Signature detail: the twitching tail. Never bloody, never truly frightening.

scene-cage.unfolded: Far: the flat plain with a thin band of green and yellow fields under a pale cream-gold sky. Middle: two or three thorny kikar trees with flat crowns, on the trailing (right) half. Near, on the trailing half: the bamboo-and-wood cage beside the dusty road, the tiger inside filling it, and the Brahman on the road just in front with staff and bundle. The leading (left) pane's upper two thirds are calm pale sky above the low line of fields.
scene-cage.folded: The cage close up: the tiger's broad face behind the bamboo bars in the middle, the Brahman's head and shoulder at one side looking at him, pale sky above for the words.

scene-pipal.unfolded: Far: the flat fields and the pale morning sky. Middle and near, on the trailing (right) half: the huge old pipal, its grey ribbed trunk rising from a low earth platform, its crown of heart-shaped leaves spreading out of the top of the picture and throwing a pool of shade over the road. The Brahman stands small in the shade, looking up, staff in hand. The leading pane's upper two thirds are open pale sky with only a few leaf tips hanging in at the top edge.
scene-pipal.folded: The Brahman in the middle, head tilted up, with the grey trunk beside him and a fringe of long-tipped heart-shaped leaves across the top of the band; pale sky between the leaves.

scene-well.unfolded: Far: pale sky over a flat line of yellow mustard. Middle: green wheat with a shining ditch running through it toward the leading pane. Near, on the trailing (right) half: the round brick well with its upright wooden wheel and loop of red clay pots spilling water, the old grey buffalo yoked to the beam mid-step on her worn circle, the Brahman beside her with a hand raised in question. The leading pane's upper two thirds are calm pale sky above the low fields.
scene-well.folded: The buffalo's head and curved horns in the middle with the wooden wheel and its clay pots behind her, the Brahman's face at one side, pale sky above.

scene-road.unfolded: Late afternoon with a PALE soft gold sky warming to peach near the horizon, never dark. Far: the mud-brick village, tiny, on the leading side, and perhaps one small paper kite. Middle: wheat on one side of the road and yellow mustard on the other. Near, on the trailing (right) half: the long pale road running away into the distance, the Brahman leaning on his staff, and the Jackal trotting up beside him with his head cocked. The leading pane's upper two thirds are open pale sky.
scene-road.folded: The Jackal in the middle looking up with his head on one side, the Brahman's face above him at one side, mustard flowers low in the band and pale gold sky above.

pictures.punjab: Five pale blue rivers winding side by side across one flat golden plain, seen from high above, coming together toward the bottom of the picture; a faint white line of far mountains at the very top is allowed here only.
pictures.priest-and-teacher: One old hand-written book of long, narrow loose pages lying open on a low carved wooden stand, on a deep plum ground. No figures, no religious image.
pictures.pipal-tree: One large heart-shaped pipal leaf with pale veins and a long thin pointed tip, hanging from a short twig, on a deep green ground.
pictures.well-wheel: One upright wooden wheel over a round brick well, with a loop of small red clay pots on ropes, the top pots tipping out bright water; no animal.

portraits.brahman: Half figure, mild and smiling, in his white shawl with the staff in one hand and the cloth bundle on his shoulder; warm pale gold behind.
portraits.jackal: The Jackal sitting, head tilted, one hind paw raised to scratch his ear, eyes half shut and a small sly smile; soft field green behind.

artBrief.cover: The moment before the door shuts: the Tiger inside the cage glaring out through the bamboo bars, the Jackal in the middle bowing low with one paw on the latch and his eyes on the reader, the Brahman a step behind with his staff; kikar trees, the dusty road and a pale gold sky behind.
